set1.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set1.q: Why must ABO antigens be matched in transfusion?
opts: Transfused cells are permanent replacements
Transfusions are described as temporary rather than as permanent cell replacements.
There are no MHC molecules on red blood cells
Correct, so ABO is the critical matching system. You carry antibodies in your serum against the antigens you lack, and mismatch can be fatal through complement activation and lysis.
MHC matching is more important than ABO for red cells
Red blood cells carry NO MHC molecules, which is what makes ABO critical.
Red cells carry the full set of HLA antigens
They do not; the absence of MHC on red cells is the stated reason ABO matters.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: 6 — Describe etiology autoimmune conditions
set1.q: Which predisposition to autoimmune conditions is described?
opts: Women are affected more than men
Correct. Women are more likely to have autoimmune conditions than men, and autoimmunities also run in families.
Men are affected more than women
It is the reverse: women are more likely than men to have autoimmune conditions.
They do not run in families
Autoimmunities DO run in families; there are genetic as well as gender predispositions.
They affect only one organ each
Disruption of function can be systemic OR organ specific, so a single-organ rule is wrong.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 52

set1.io: 6 — Describe etiology autoimmune conditions
set1.q: Which viruses are linked to the onset of type 1 diabetes?
opts: Mumps virus and the measles virus
Mumps appears only as a naturally oncolytic virus; the diabetes triggers are coxsackie, echovirus and rubella.
Coxsackie virus, echovirus and rubella
Correct. Coxsackie viruses A and B, echovirus and rubella are listed as triggers of type 1 diabetes through a normal immune response.
Hepatitis B virus and papillomavirus
These are oncogenic viruses, linked to liver cancer and cervical carcinoma, not to type 1 diabetes.
Human herpesvirus 8 and Epstein-Barr virus
These are oncogenic viruses, linked to Kaposi's sarcoma and Burkitt's lymphoma, rather than to autoimmune diabetes.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 54

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: Which are named as infectious allergy examples of type IV?
opts: Tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis and histoplasmosis
Correct, with toxoplasmosis and candidiasis completing the list — chronic infections where the T cell response itself damages tissue.
Hay fever and anaphylaxis
Hay fever and anaphylaxis are type I, IgE mediated and immediate rather than delayed and cellular.
Transfusion reactions and hemolytic disease of the newborn
Those are type II, involving antibody against cell surface antigens.
Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction
Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction are type III, mediated by immune complexes.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 40

set1.io: 7 — Differentiate between primary and secondary immunodeficiency conditions
set1.q: A young boy has recurrent bacterial infections and no detectable antibodies. Which defect is most likely?
opts: A T cell defect
T cell defects such as DiGeorge syndrome bring recurrent fungal, protozoan, helminth and viral infections instead.
An acquired viral infection
A virus such as the human immunodeficiency virus causes SECONDARY immunodeficiency by targeting T helper cells, not congenital absence of antibody.
A mast cell defect
Mast cells mediate allergy; recurrent bacterial infection with no antibody points to B cells.
A B cell defect
Correct. Agammaglobulinemia is a B cell defect; the patient lacks antibodies and suffers more bacterial infections.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 63

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: Which are the general targets of a type I reaction?
opts: Bone marrow and lymph nodes
Those are sites of immune cell production rather than targets of the allergic response.
Liver and spleen
Neither liver nor spleen is among the general targets named for a type I reaction.
Joints and kidneys
Joint and kidney involvement is typical of immune complex disease, type III.
Skin, airway, gut and conjunctiva
Correct, producing rashes, itching, redness, rhinitis, sneezing, diarrhea and tears respectively.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What is the Arthus reaction?
opts: Localized dermal injury from inflamed blood vessels
Correct — a vasculitis, typically following a second injection of vaccine at a site, and normally self limiting.
A systemic reaction to foreign animal protein
That is serum sickness, which deposits complexes in heart, kidneys, skin and joints.
A delayed T cell response to an injected antigen
The Arthus reaction is immune complex mediated, type III, rather than T cell mediated.
An immediate wheal and flare
An immediate wheal and flare is the type I reaction from mast cell degranulation.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 39

set1.io: 9 — Compare and contrast immunotherapy strategies
set1.q: Bacillus Calmette-Guérin is used to treat which cancer?
opts: Kidney cancer
Metastatic kidney cancer is treated with interleukin 2 (aldesleukin).
Bladder cancer
Correct. Bacillus Calmette-Guérin, a weakened form of the tuberculosis organism, stimulates a general immune response and is used to treat bladder cancer.
Prostate cancer
Prostate cancer is treated with sipuleucel-T, approved for metastatic castration-resistant disease.
Cervical cancer
Cervical cancer is PREVENTED by the papillomavirus vaccine, a prophylactic vaccine.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 81

set1.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
set1.q: A surgeon harvests a vein from a patient's own leg to bypass a blocked artery. Which graft type is this?
opts: An allograft
An allograft comes from a different person of the same species, which would carry foreign antigens.
A xenograft
A xenograft comes from another species, not from the patient's own tissue.
An autograft
Correct. An autograft is a self graft; skin, gum and vein grafts moved within one patient are the examples given.
An isograft
An isograft comes from a genetically identical twin rather than from the patient's own body.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 43

set1.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set1.q: What are the consequences of a transfusion reaction?
opts: Red cell destruction, glomerular blockage, fever and jaundice
Correct, and even where complement activation is incomplete, antibody-coated cells may attract natural killer cells or macrophages.
Immune complex deposition in joints and skin
Immune complex deposition in joints and skin belongs to type III rather than to transfusion.
Delayed T cell infiltration of the transfused tissue
That would be a type IV mechanism; transfusion reactions are type II.
Bronchial smooth muscle contraction
Bronchial smooth muscle contraction is the acute asthmatic response in type I allergy.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 35

set1.io: 1 — Describe the types of immunopathologies
set1.q: Which hypersensitivity types are B cell mediated?
opts: Types I, II and III
Correct, and type IV is the exception — it is T cell mediated, which is why it is delayed rather than immediate.
Types I and II only
Type III is also antibody driven, through immune complexes of IgG and IgM.
Type IV only
Type IV is the T CELL mediated one, standing apart from the other three.
All four types
Type IV is T cell mediated rather than B cell mediated, which is what sets it apart.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 3

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: How many IgE molecules can each mast cell bind?
opts: Between 10,000 and 40,000
Correct, which explains the scale of the response — a single cell carries an enormous number of trigger points for crosslinking.
Between 10 and 40
The figure is three orders of magnitude larger, at 10,000 to 40,000.
Exactly one
Crosslinking requires many bound antibodies, and each cell binds tens of thousands.
Between 100 and 400
The number given is 10,000 to 40,000 IgE molecules per cell, not hundreds.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: 6 — Describe etiology autoimmune conditions
set1.q: Premature aging of the thymus is characteristic of which group?
opts: Young people with autoimmune disorders
Correct. Premature thymic aging is characteristic of young people with autoimmune disorders, and chronic inflammation may hasten it.
Adults who received bone marrow grafts
Marrow recipients are at risk of graft versus host disease; premature thymic aging is described in young people with autoimmunity.
Children with helminth infections
Helminth infection is discussed in the hygiene hypothesis, not as a cause of premature thymic aging.
Mothers sensitized to the Rh antigen
Rh sensitization concerns hemolytic disease of the newborn, not thymic aging.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 57

set1.io: 9 — Compare and contrast immunotherapy strategies
set1.q: How do immune checkpoint inhibitors work?
opts: They kill cancer cells directly
Checkpoint inhibitors do NOT kill cancer cells directly; they help target them for immune cells.
They return engineered T cells
Engineering a patient's cells and returning them is ADOPTIVE CELL THERAPY, such as chimeric antigen receptor T cells.
They infect and lyse tumor cells
Infecting and lysing tumor cells is ONCOLYTIC VIRAL THERAPY.
They block the T cell off signal
Correct. They stop checkpoint proteins binding their partners, preventing the off signal so T cells keep killing cancer cells.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 74

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What does the hygiene hypothesis propose?
opts: Exposure to allergens in childhood causes lifelong allergy
The hypothesis runs the opposite way, attributing allergy to too LITTLE early immune challenge.
Hygiene practices directly damage epithelial barriers
The proposed mechanism concerns regulation of the immune system rather than barrier damage.
Vaccination produces IgE against vaccine components
Vaccination is named among the things that reduced parasitic infection rather than as a source of IgE.
Underused immune systems are less successfully regulated
Correct. Better hygiene, vaccination and antibiotics eradicated helminth and other parasitic infections in Western Europe and North America, leaving the system without its usual training.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 7

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: What are the systemic targets of a type I reaction?
opts: Red blood cells and platelets
Those are targets in type II reactions such as transfusion incompatibility.
Basement membranes of epithelial tissue
Basement membranes of epithelial tissue are where type III immune complexes deposit instead.
Smooth muscle, mucous glands, nerve
Correct, and the responses are vascular dilation and constriction, producing changes in blood pressure and respiration.
Skin, conjunctiva and nasal mucosa
Those are among the GENERAL targets rather than the systemic ones.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 12

set1.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
set1.q: Graft versus host disease is which hypersensitivity type?
opts: Type III
Type III is immune complex disease, the mechanism of chronic rejection rather than graft versus host disease.
Type IV
Correct. Graft versus host disease is type IV: donor T cells in the graft attack the recipient's tissues.
Type I
Type I is immunoglobulin E mediated immediate allergy, not a T cell attack on host tissue.
Type II
Type II is antibody against cell surface antigen, the mechanism of hyperacute rejection rather than graft versus host disease.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
set1.q: What is immune surveillance?
opts: Tissue typing before a transplant
Tissue typing of human leukocyte antigen antigens is done to reduce graft rejection, not to control cancer.
Skin prick testing for allergies
Skin prick testing diagnoses type I allergy through wheal and flare reactions.
Immunity keeping cancer in check
Correct. Immune surveillance is the immune system keeping cancer in check, which is why its failure allows tumors to establish.
Screening blood donors for ABO type
ABO typing and cross-matching belong to transfusion, not to the immune system's control of cancer.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 66

set1.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set1.q: What does prevention of allergy involve?
opts: Taking antihistamines daily regardless of exposure
Taking antihistamines regardless of exposure is pharmacological control rather than prevention.
Injecting small amounts of the allergen
Injecting small amounts of allergen is desensitization, the third of the three approaches.
Administering epinephrine prophylactically
Epinephrine is used to reverse an acute reaction rather than to prevent exposure.
Modifying environment and behavior
Correct, and it is listed first because removing the trigger is the only approach that does not depend on blunting a normal mechanism. The aim is to avoid the allergen entirely.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 27

set1.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
set1.q: Hepatitis B virus is associated with which cancer?
opts: Kaposi's sarcoma
Kaposi's sarcoma is associated with human herpesvirus 8 and the human immunodeficiency virus.
Hepatocellular carcinoma
Correct. Hepatitis B virus is associated with liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, which is why its vaccine is a prophylactic cancer vaccine.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is associated with Epstein-Barr virus.
Cervical carcinoma
Cervical carcinoma is associated with papillomavirus, which also causes benign genital warts.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 68

set1.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set1.q: What is the most common form of allergen specific immunotherapy?
opts: Inhaled allergen challenge
Inhaled challenge is not among the described desensitization routes.
Subcutaneous immunotherapy
Correct — small amounts of allergen introduced by injection, improving reactions in about 80 percent of those who complete the process.
Sublingual immunotherapy
Sublingual immunotherapy is used more in other parts of the world than in the United States.
Intravenous allergen infusion
The named routes are subcutaneous injection and sublingual administration.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 29

set1.io: 7 — Differentiate between primary and secondary immunodeficiency conditions
set1.q: An infant with an absent thymus has recurrent fungal and viral infections. Which condition fits?
opts: Graft versus host disease
Graft versus host disease follows transplantation, when donor T cells attack the host.
Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease of the thyroid, not a congenital absence of the thymus.
DiGeorge syndrome
Correct. DiGeorge syndrome is a T cell defect with a missing or abnormal thymus, and it brings fungal, protozoan, helminth and viral infections.
Agammaglobulinemia
Agammaglobulinemia is a B cell defect with absent antibodies and recurrent BACTERIAL infections.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 63

set1.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
set1.q: Which is a possible cause of cancer?
opts: Overactive thymic selection
The thymus is linked to autoimmunity through its aging; overactive selection is not a listed cause of cancer.
Activation of oncogenes
Correct. Errors in mitosis, genetic damage, activation of oncogenes and retroviruses are the possible causes listed; all disrupt the normal cell division cycle.
Loss of immunoglobulin E
Immunoglobulin E mediates allergy; its loss is not a cause of cancer.
Excess regulatory T cell death
Regulatory T cells in a tumor actually worsen prognosis; their death is not listed as a cause of cancer.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 66

set1.io: 1 — Describe the types of immunopathologies
set1.q: Which four categories of immunopathology are described?
opts: Bacterial, viral, fungal and parasitic disease
These classify pathogens rather than describing ways the immune system itself goes wrong.
Innate, adaptive, humoral and cellular
These are divisions of normal immune function rather than categories of immunopathology.
Allergy, autoimmunity, immunodeficiency and cancer
Correct, and they sort neatly by direction: allergy and autoimmunity are overreactions, while immunodeficiency and cancer are underreactions.
Infection, inflammation, necrosis and repair
These are general tissue responses rather than the four categories of immune system malfunction named.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 3

set1.io: 6 — Describe etiology autoimmune conditions
set1.q: Reactive arthritis follows infection with which organisms?
opts: Coxsackie virus, echovirus and rubella
These viruses are linked to type 1 diabetes, another autoimmune result of a normal immune response.
Borrelia burgdorferi and group A strep
Borrelia causes Lyme disease arthritis and streptococci cause rheumatic fever; reactive arthritis follows enteric bacteria.
Epstein-Barr virus and a retrovirus
Earlier Epstein-Barr or retroviral infection is associated with multiple sclerosis, not reactive arthritis.
Shigella, Salmonella and Campylobacter
Correct. Reactive arthritis is an autoimmune result of a normal immune response to Shigella, Salmonella or Campylobacter.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 54

set1.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set1.q: How many people are heavily and persistently infected with helminths?
opts: About ten thousand
The burden described is of the order of one billion people heavily and persistently infected.
Fewer than one hundred thousand
Helminth infection is endemic across tropical countries, affecting around one billion heavily.
About one billion
Correct, in countries where helminth infection is endemic — and notably those populations do not show corresponding allergic disease.
About one million
The figure given is a thousand times larger, at around one billion.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 7

set1.io: 6 — Describe etiology autoimmune conditions
set1.q: A child develops arthritis and myocarditis after a streptococcal infection. What is the mechanism?
opts: Streptococci directly invade heart muscle
The damage is immune mediated cross-reactivity, not direct invasion of the heart by the organism.
Donor T cells attack the child's joints
Donor T cells attacking tissue is graft versus host disease, which requires a transplant.
A missing thymus leaves T cells unchecked
An absent or abnormal thymus is DiGeorge syndrome, a primary immunodeficiency, not rheumatic fever.
Strep antibodies cross-react with heart
Correct. This is rheumatic fever: the streptococcal cell wall stimulates antibodies, and some cross-react with heart tissue, a molecular mimicry reaction.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 54

set1.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
set1.q: What does a high number of regulatory T cells in a tumor predict?
opts: Imminent graft rejection
Graft rejection concerns transplants; regulatory T cells here are being recruited by a tumor.
A worse prognosis
Correct. Regulatory T cells release transforming growth factor beta and interleukin 10, suppressing tumor-specific T cells; the more there are, the worse the prognosis.
A better prognosis
Regulatory T cells SUPPRESS the anti-tumor response, so more of them predicts a worse outcome.
No change in prognosis
Their number matters: more regulatory T cells in a tumor means a worse prognosis.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 72

set1.io: 7 — Differentiate between primary and secondary immunodeficiency conditions
set1.q: What distinguishes a primary immunodeficiency from a secondary one?
opts: It always follows a viral infection
Viral causes such as the human immunodeficiency virus produce SECONDARY immunodeficiency.
It involves only the complement system
Primary deficiencies can involve B cells, T cells, phagocytes or complement, not complement alone.
It is congenital, usually genetic
Correct. Primary immunodeficiency is congenital and usually genetic; secondary immunodeficiency is acquired after birth from natural or artificial agents.
It is acquired after birth from a drug
Acquisition after birth, from natural or artificial agents such as drugs, defines SECONDARY immunodeficiency.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 62

set1.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
set1.q: What is a graft taken from a genetically identical twin called?
opts: An isograft
Correct. An isograft comes from a genetically identical twin, so donor and recipient share the same histocompatibility antigens.
An autograft
An autograft is taken from the patient's own body, such as a skin, gum or vein graft, rather than from a twin.
An allograft
An allograft comes from a genetically different member of the same species, so it carries foreign histocompatibility antigens.
A xenograft
A xenograft comes from another species entirely, which is the least compatible source of the four graft types.
set1.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 43

set2.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set2.q: How is hemolytic disease of the newborn prevented?
opts: Passive immunization with anti-Rh antibody
Correct — Rhogam prevents sensitization of the mother, which is why it must be given before her own response can develop.
Active immunization of the mother against Rh
The approach is PASSIVE immunization, giving preformed antibody rather than provoking her own.
Transfusing the mother with Rh positive blood
Transfusing the mother with Rh positive blood would sensitize her rather than protect her.
Cross-matching the fetus against the mother
Cross-matching is a transfusion compatibility test rather than a preventive measure here.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 36

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What do basophils initiate?
opts: Complement activation by the classical pathway
Complement activation characterizes types II and III rather than the basophil's initiating role.
Cytotoxic T cell proliferation
Cytotoxic T cells belong to type IV responses rather than to the basophil-driven IgE axis.
A TH2 response and production of IgE
Correct. They are rare granulocytes, and in normal defense they act against helminths — the same axis that produces allergy when misdirected.
A TH1 response and production of IgG
The response they initiate is TH2 with IgE, which is the allergic axis.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
set2.q: Some tumor cells cleave a stress molecule that natural killer cells recognize and release it in soluble form. What is the effect?
opts: Natural killer cells destroy it faster
Normally surface stress molecules mark the cell for killing; shedding them in soluble form blocks that recognition.
Complement lyses the tumor cell
The mechanism shown involves lymphocyte receptors, not complement lysis.
Mast cells degranulate at the tumor
Mast cell degranulation is the effector step of type I allergy, not of tumor evasion.
The tumor cell escapes being killed
Correct. The soluble molecule binds the killing receptor on natural killer and gamma-delta T cells, so the variant tumor cell is not killed and proliferates.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 71

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: How do corticosteroids act in allergy?
opts: They inhibit lymphocytes to reduce IgE
Correct, acting upstream on the production of the antibody rather than on the mediators it releases.
They block mast cell degranulation
Blocking mast cell degranulation is what cromolyn sodium does rather than a corticosteroid.
They bind histamine receptors on target organs
Binding histamine receptors on target organs is the antihistamine mechanism.
They block leukotriene synthesis
Blocking leukotriene synthesis is montelukast sodium rather than a corticosteroid.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 28

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What is the acute response in allergic asthma?
opts: Cytokine and eosinophil granule mediated inflammation
Cytokine and eosinophil granule mediated inflammation describes the CHRONIC phase, which is type IV.
Immune complex deposition in the alveolar membrane
That would be a type III mechanism rather than the acute asthmatic response.
Complement-mediated lysis of airway epithelium
Complement lysis of epithelium characterizes type II rather than the acute asthmatic response.
Bronchial smooth muscle contraction with increased mucus
Correct, producing airway obstruction. It is triggered by inhaled allergen crosslinking specific IgE on mast cell surfaces.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: 9 — Compare and contrast immunotherapy strategies
set2.q: An antibody against CD20 is conjugated to a radionuclide. How does it kill malignant B cells?
opts: It removes the T cell off signal
Removing the off signal is how checkpoint inhibitors work, not radionuclide conjugates.
It replicates inside the tumor
Replication inside tumor cells is how oncolytic viruses work; an antibody does not replicate.
Radiation damages their genome
Correct. The radioactive antibody binds the malignant B cells and irradiates them, and the radiation damages their deoxyribonucleic acid and kills them.
It blocks their mitotic spindle
Blocking the mitotic spindle is how the anti-CD30 conjugate works, releasing auristatin inside lymphoma cells.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 77

set2.io: 9 — Compare and contrast immunotherapy strategies
set2.q: What is the current status of tumor infiltrating lymphocyte therapy?
opts: Abandoned after the 1890s
Falling from favor after the 1890s describes Coley's toxins, displaced by radiation and chemotherapy.
In development, not yet approved
Correct. Tumor infiltrating lymphocytes, cytotoxic T cells expanded to a therapeutic amount, are still in development and not yet approved.
Approved for different blood cancers
Approval for blood cancers belongs to chimeric antigen receptor T cells.
Approved for metastatic melanoma only
Melanoma is named for checkpoint inhibitors, interleukin 2, interferon alpha and one oncolytic virus, not for tumor infiltrating lymphocytes.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 75

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: What is omalizumab?
opts: A monoclonal antibody against IgE
Correct, so it removes the antibody that arms the mast cell rather than acting on the cell or its mediators.
A leukotriene synthesis blocker
Blocking leukotriene synthesis is montelukast sodium rather than an anti-IgE antibody.
A histamine receptor blocker
Blocking histamine receptors on target organs describes the antihistamines.
A mast cell stabilizer
Blocking degranulation is what cromolyn sodium does rather than an antibody against IgE.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 28

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: Which hypersensitivity type is chronic asthma?
opts: Type III
Type III is immune complex mediated, as in serum sickness, rather than the chronic asthma mechanism.
Type IV
Correct, mediated by cytokines and eosinophil granules — so a single disease can begin as type I and become type IV as it becomes chronic.
Type I
Type I is the ACUTE asthmatic response; chronic asthma is type IV, cytokine and eosinophil driven.
Type II
Type II involves antibody against cell surface antigens, as in transfusion reactions.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: 1 — Describe the types of immunopathologies
set2.q: Why is cancer described as both a cause and an effect of immune dysfunction?
opts: Immune failure permits it; the tumor then suppresses immunity
Correct. Immune surveillance normally keeps cancer in check, and successful tumors evade and actively manipulate the response once established.
Cancer cells are destroyed only by antibody
Tumor defense involves cytotoxic cells and surveillance rather than antibody alone.
Cancer only arises in people with no immune system
Cancer arises in immunocompetent people too; surveillance reduces rather than eliminates the risk.
Cancer is classified as an overreaction of immunity
Cancer is grouped with immunodeficiency as an UNDERreaction rather than with the overreactions.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 3

set2.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
set2.q: How does chronic rejection cause a graft to fail?
opts: Thickened vessel walls starve it
Correct. Immune complexes in the vessel walls recruit inflammatory cells, the walls thicken, and the graft's blood supply becomes inadequate.
Preexisting antibodies cause hemorrhage
Hemorrhage from preexisting antibody is HYPERACUTE rejection, which happens right after grafting rather than years later.
Donor T cells attack the recipient's skin
Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue is graft versus host disease, not chronic rejection of the graft itself.
Immunoglobulin E triggers mast cells
Immunoglobulin E and mast cells are type I allergy; chronic rejection is a type III immune complex process.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 47

set2.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
set2.q: In acute rejection of a kidney, where do the graft's dendritic cells go to activate effector T cells?
opts: The renal pelvis
The renal pelvis is part of the graft's collecting system; the dendritic cells leave the kidney for the spleen.
The spleen
Correct. Dendritic cells carried in the graft migrate to the spleen, activate effector T cells there, and those T cells return via the blood to destroy the graft.
The thymus
The thymus is where T cells mature, not where graft dendritic cells activate effector T cells during acute rejection.
The bone marrow
Bone marrow produces blood cell precursors; the dendritic cells from the graft travel to the spleen instead.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 46

set2.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
set2.q: A patient receives a heart valve taken from a pig. Which graft type is this?
opts: An allograft
An allograft comes from another member of the SAME species; a pig valve in a human crosses species.
An isograft
An isograft comes from a genetically identical twin, which a pig donor clearly is not.
An autograft
An autograft is the patient's own tissue moved to a new site, such as a vein graft from the leg.
A xenograft
Correct. A xenograft is tissue from another species, here a pig transplanted into a human.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 43

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What is said about the relationship between the portal of entry and the organ affected?
opts: They are always the same
The organ of allergic expression may differ from the portal of entry.
They are never the same
They may be the same; the point is that this is not guaranteed.
The portal determines the severity but not the site
The statement concerns whether the site matches the portal rather than severity.
They may or may not be the same
Correct, which is why an ingested food allergen can produce urticaria in the skin — antigen entering blood vessels is carried there.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 10

set2.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
set2.q: Graft success depends mainly on compatibility of which molecules?
opts: Toll-like pattern receptors
Pattern receptors recognize microbial molecules; transplant compatibility is judged on major histocompatibility complex molecules.
Histocompatibility antigens
Correct. Rejection is associated with the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), and different grafts succeed to different degrees because of major histocompatibility complex compatibility.
Complement regulatory proteins
Complement contributes to some rejection damage, but graft matching is based on the major histocompatibility complex.
Immunoglobulin E receptors
Receptors for immunoglobulin E arm mast cells in type I allergy; they are not the basis of tissue matching.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 43

set2.io: 6 — Describe etiology autoimmune conditions
set2.q: Autoantibodies bind receptors on thyroid follicle cells and raise thyroxine levels. Which disease is this?
opts: Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis damages the myelin sheath of nerve cells rather than stimulating the thyroid.
Graves' disease
Correct. In Graves' disease autoantibodies attach to receptors on the follicle cells that secrete thyroxine, increasing it and causing hyperthyroidism.
Hashimoto's thyroiditis
Hashimoto's thyroiditis DESTROYS follicle cells through autoantibodies and T cells, lowering thyroxine.
Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis autoantibodies bind acetylcholine receptors, causing muscle weakness rather than hyperthyroidism.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 61

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What is familial about allergy?
opts: The route by which allergens enter
Portal of entry is determined by exposure rather than inherited.
Nothing — allergy has no familial component
A generalized predisposition to allergies is specifically described as familial.
A generalized predisposition
Correct — families inherit the tendency rather than the particular allergen, which is why relatives may react to entirely different things. The specific allergy is not inherited.
The specific allergen a person reacts to
The inherited element is the general predisposition rather than the specific allergy.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 8

set2.io: 7 — Differentiate between primary and secondary immunodeficiency conditions
set2.q: Which is a secondary immunodeficiency?
opts: Congenital agammaglobulinemia
Congenital agammaglobulinemia is a PRIMARY B cell immunodeficiency.
Severe combined immunodeficiency
Severe combined immunodeficiency is congenital, a PRIMARY defect of both lymphocyte limbs.
Suppression after chemotherapy
Correct. Chemotherapy, radiation, infection such as the human immunodeficiency virus, and blood cell cancers cause secondary immunodeficiency after birth.
DiGeorge syndrome from birth
DiGeorge syndrome is congenital, a PRIMARY T cell immunodeficiency.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 65

set2.io: 9 — Compare and contrast immunotherapy strategies
set2.q: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are currently used for which cancers?
opts: Melanoma and lung cancer
Correct. Some checkpoint inhibitors are currently used for melanoma and some lung cancers.
Bladder cancer only
Bladder cancer is treated with bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), a therapeutic vaccine, not named for checkpoint inhibitors.
Prostate cancer only
Sipuleucel-T, a therapeutic vaccine, is the agent approved for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer.
Blood cancers only
Chimeric antigen receptor T cells are the therapy approved for different blood cancers.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 74

set2.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
set2.q: What is required for a type III reaction to occur?
opts: Prior sensitization with IgE
IgE sensitization is the type I mechanism, in which cell-bound antibody is crosslinked by allergen.
A T cell mediated memory response
T cell memory drives type IV rather than immune complex disease.
Only a trace of antigen
A LARGE amount of antigen is specified, which is why serum sickness follows bulk protein exposure.
A large amount of antigen
Correct, which is part of why serum sickness follows exposure to foreign animal proteins in quantity rather than to a trace allergen.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 38

set2.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
set2.q: About what share of bone marrow recipients develop graft versus host disease?
opts: About 90%
Most recipients escape it; graft versus host disease affects about 30% of marrow recipients.
About 30%
Correct. Graft versus host disease affects about 30% of marrow recipients, reflecting marrow's sensitivity to human leukocyte antigen discrepancies.
About 3%
The figure is ten times higher: about 30% of marrow recipients are affected.
About 60%
That doubles the true figure; about 30% of marrow recipients develop graft versus host disease.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 49

set2.io: 7 — Differentiate between primary and secondary immunodeficiency conditions
set2.q: Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes which kind of immunodeficiency?
opts: Severe combined immunodeficiency
Correct. Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes some types of severe combined immunodeficiency, a congenital, primary defect.
A secondary immunodeficiency
Adenosine deaminase deficiency is congenital, which makes it PRIMARY rather than acquired after birth.
An isolated complement defect
Adenosine deaminase deficiency damages lymphocytes, producing combined immunodeficiency rather than a complement defect.
An autoimmune thyroid disease
Adenosine deaminase deficiency is an immunodeficiency, an underreaction, not an autoimmune overreaction.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 64

set2.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
set2.q: What does cromolyn sodium do?
opts: Reverses airway constriction directly
That is epinephrine, which also re-establishes endothelial tight junctions.
Blocks degranulation
Correct — it prevents the mast cell from releasing its granule contents rather than blocking the mediators afterwards.
Reduces IgE production by inhibiting lymphocytes
Reducing IgE production by inhibiting lymphocytes is the corticosteroid mechanism.
Binds to IgE as a monoclonal antibody
Binding IgE as a monoclonal antibody describes omalizumab rather than cromolyn sodium.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 28

set2.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
set2.q: Which exposures can activate oncogenes?
opts: Horse serum, animal drugs or hormones
Foreign animal proteins cause serum sickness, a type III reaction, not oncogene activation.
Metals, cosmetics or poison ivy
These cause contact dermatitis, a type IV reaction, not oncogene activation.
Radiation, chemicals or viruses
Correct. Oncogenes may be activated by exposure to radiation, chemicals or oncogenic viruses during transformation.
Pollen, dust mites or animal dander
These are allergens that trigger type I hypersensitivity, not agents that activate oncogenes.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 67

set2.io: 9 — Compare and contrast immunotherapy strategies
set2.q: What is the main challenge of oncolytic viral therapy?
opts: No virus is naturally oncolytic
Some viruses are naturally oncolytic, such as mumps, while others are engineered.
Immunity may clear the virus first
Correct. The immune system may wipe out the oncolytic virus before it does its job, and only a few are approved, just one in the United States, for melanoma.
The virus destroys normal cells
Oncolytic viruses infect normal cells but cannot replicate in them, so normal cells are left largely undamaged.
The virus cannot infect tumor cells
The virus does infect and replicate in tumor cells, lysing them and releasing progeny.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 80

set2.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
set2.q: From what does a cancer arise?
opts: One cell with a single mutation
One mutation is not enough; transformation requires accumulated multiple mutations.
Immune cells that lose tolerance
Loss of tolerance describes autoimmunity; cancer arises from a single mutated cell.
One cell with multiple mutations
Correct. A cancer arises from a single cell that has accumulated multiple mutations, with oncogenes activated by radiation, chemicals or oncogenic viruses.
Many cells with one shared mutation
The origin is a SINGLE cell, and it needs multiple mutations rather than one.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 67

set2.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
set2.q: When does an Rh negative person produce anti-Rh antibodies?
opts: Whenever they encounter any foreign protein
Sensitization is specific, through bad transfusion or incompatible pregnancy.
Only if they are also ABO incompatible
Rh sensitization is independent of ABO grouping and requires prior exposure to Rh positive cells.
Only after sensitization
Correct — unlike ABO, where antibodies against the antigens you lack are already present, Rh requires prior exposure. A bad transfusion or an incompatible pregnancy does it.
From birth, without any exposure
Rh negative individuals do NOT produce anti-Rh antibodies unless sensitized.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 36

set2.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
set2.q: Where are tumor specific antigens found?
opts: On tumor cells only
Correct. Tumor specific antigens are present on tumor cells but not on normal cells, derived from viral proteins or mutated cellular proteins.
On tumor and normal cells alike
Presence on tumor cells AND, in smaller amounts, normal cells describes tumor ASSOCIATED antigens.
Only on normal cells near a tumor
The antigens are defined by their presence on tumor cells, not on neighboring normal tissue.
Only on red blood cells
Red cell antigens belong to the ABO and Rh systems of transfusion, not to tumor antigens.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 70

set2.io: 1 — Describe the types of immunopathologies
set2.q: How is allergy or hypersensitivity defined?
opts: A response using mechanisms unique to allergic disease
The mechanisms are the same as those used in protective immunity; only the target and the magnitude differ.
An abnormal response directed against self antigens
That is autoimmunity, which is directed at self rather than at an external allergen.
A loss or deficiency of immune function
That is immunodeficiency, an underreaction rather than an overreaction.
An exaggerated, misdirected immune response to an allergen
Correct, and the critical point is that it uses the SAME mechanisms as protective immune reactions — nothing novel is happening, it is simply happening against the wrong target.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 3

set2.io: 6 — Describe etiology autoimmune conditions
set2.q: Autoimmunity involves which hypersensitivity types?
opts: Type I only
Type I is the one hypersensitivity NOT involved in autoimmunity.
All four types
Type I is excluded; autoimmune disease uses types II, III and IV.
Type IV only
Type IV is one of three involved; types II and III also cause autoimmune disease.
All except type I
Correct. Autoimmunity involves types II, III and IV, but not type I, the immunoglobulin E mediated allergy.
set2.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 52
